transcript: last night I saw the new film adaptation of Matilda on Netflix. and for context, I saw the show on Broadway in early previews and it rocked my world. I quickly became obsessed with it. I was beyond furious that it lost the Tony Awards to Kinky Boots, but I've actually been pretty and different about this film version. up till now, I just kind of assumed it would be bad. I don't know, I feel like we've been burned so much recently that the idea that it could actually capture some of the magic of the stage version literally did not even cross my mind. but yeah, I actually thought this was pretty great. it has a lot of the same sharp humor and emotional maturity as the stage version. and it also just reminded me why I loved it so much. not just because of the brilliant score, but also the adaptation. I think what Dennis Kelly did by strategically deepening and expanding on the original story is extremely impressive. there were a lot of cuts and even some additions to the script. I didn't really have any major issues with any of them. maybe some quibbles here and there, but nothing too egregious. and in fact, in some cases I thought it was an improvement. one thing I noticed is that this adaptation seems to have a lot of focus on matilda's righteous anger, which is an element that's definitely there in other versions of the story. including the musical. but it feels even more emphasized here. and in general, I think the cuts to the script help to streamline the narrative in a way that makes it more. feel more like a continuous rise intention, so that matilda's frustration and the children's frustration feels like it's constantly building to this inevitable breaking point. I think my only major issue was the look of the movie, which, you know, I get it. you could say, like, oh, it fits with the zingy, fantastical world of the story, and I. it's. that's fair. but to me, it just kind of came across like an unfortunate combination of, like, low budget CGI and green screen with a director who's clearly more accustomed to working on the stage. also, like, I was very much raised on Roald Dahl, but in the last few years, I have learned about how he was just a really terrible person and how his bigotry definitely feels baked into a lot of his stories. and that none of the adaptations really try to meaningfully address it, including this one. I think for Matilda, it's the fatphobia especially, and Roald dahl's general tendency to associate characters morality with their physical appearance. I will say, though, I think it was the right decision to not cast a man as Trunchbull, as much as I really loved Bertie carville's performance as Trunchbull on Broadway. but there's a lot to unpack there. and for a few reasons, I think they made the right call here. overall, though, this definitely worked for me. and I'm sure I'm biased because I was so attached to the stage version, but I was prepared not to like it. and I was pretty delighted by how much of the inventiveness and jubalance and emotional depth came through in this version.
classificationReason: This is a review of the Matilda film adaptation on Netflix, not a stage production. Creator mentions seeing the Broadway show in previews as context but is primarily reviewing the movie version.
